extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy studying Aristotelian ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and exposition of Aristotle's account of Science (episteme), Practical Wisdom (phronesis), Judgement, Virtue, and defects of moral character (e.g., akrasia/self-control). Useful for interpreting and applying Aristotelian virtue-ethics distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science (episteme) as the most accurate Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Science must mean the most accurate of all Knowledge; the Scientific man must not merely know deductions from First Principles but possess truth respecting the First Principles. Science is equivalent to Intuition and Knowledge and has for its objects those things most precious in their nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science concerns knowledge of first principles and ultimate causes; it is 'Knowledge of the most precious objects, with a head on.' Science is contrasted with Practical Wisdom because it deals with universal, necessary principles rather than particular, contingent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom (phronesis) definition and object
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom is employed upon human matters — those which are objects of deliberation — and concerns particulars that have some definite End and a good resulting from moral action. The practically-wise person deliberates well and has capacity for attaining the practical goods best for man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical Wisdom is apt to act; it requires knowledge of particulars as well as of general principles (and, if forced, particulars are more important than principles). Its function is to calculate and deliberate about what conduces to human good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science versus Practical Wisdom (distinct faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science and Practical Wisdom cannot be identical: Science deals with universal first principles and demonstration, while Practical Wisdom is concerned with what is expedient for humans and particular facts known by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if man is superior to other animals, that does not make Practical Wisdom identical with Science. Practical Wisdom belongs to a different part of the soul and is produced by experience and time; Science is based on demonstrative reasoning from indemonstrable premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Counsel (rightness of deliberation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Counsel is the rightness of deliberation — a rightness of intellectual operation in inquiry and calculation about what to do. It is not Knowledge, Opinion, or Happy Conjecture, but 'Rightness in respect of what conduces to a given End.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good Counsel must be with reference to what is expedient: one must have a proper end, pursue it in a right manner and at the right time. It can be general (right toward the End in general) or particular (right toward a specific End). Happy Conjecture and quick perception differ because deliberation is slow and investigatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Intuition (sense for particulars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Intuition is the 'Sense' (not one of the five senses) by which we grasp the particular facts that serve as minor premisses in practical reasoning; it corresponds to the perception that a triangle is the ultimate rectilinear figure in mathematics but applied to contingent particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are two kinds of Intuition: the one taking in immutable first terms for demonstrative reasonings, the other used in practical matters taking in contingent particulars (the minor premiss). Practical Intuition is often regarded as a natural gift developed by experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciousness and equitable judgement (yvwix-q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judiciousness is the aptitude to judge well concerning matters that are proper objects of Practical Wisdom (things about which a man might doubt and deliberate). The faculty called yvwix-q denotes the right judgement of the equitable man who 'makes allowance' and attains the True in equitable decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judiciousness is neither identical with Knowledge nor any specific science; it consists in employing the opinionative faculty well when another enunciates matters within Practical Wisdom's province. It pertains particularly to moral action and particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme vs subordinate Practical Wisdom (social scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom exerted upon a community divides into a Supreme faculty (Legislation) and a subordinate faculty concerned with details (action and deliberation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subordinate functions (commonly named ttoXtiku) include Action and Deliberation — the enactment is a matter of action — while the Supreme faculty legislates about the good of the community. Other domains: Domestic Management, Executive Government (Deliberative and Judicial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom requires experience and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom's object is particular facts which come to be known from experience; therefore the young (who lack experience) cannot be possessed of Practical Wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics can be learned young because it abstracts; principles of natural philosophy must be gained by experiment and length of time; practical wisdom comes from accumulated experience and the development of practical intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of error in practical deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Error in practical matters attaches either to the general rule (major premiss) in deliberation or to the particular fact (minor premiss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a false general rule 'All water of a certain gravity is bad' or a false particular fact 'this water is of that gravity' produce wrong action. Thus both levels must be attended to in practical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom versus Cleverness (deftness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleverness is the faculty able to attain any given purpose by adapting means to ends; Practical Wisdom is not identical with Cleverness because it requires moral goodness — the right aim as well as the right means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleverness can be used for good or evil; Practical Wisdom presupposes goodness because Vice distorts moral vision and misfills the major premiss ('this is the End and the Chief Good'). Hence one cannot be Practically-Wise without being good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Virtue versus Matured (acquired) Virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between Natural Virtue (dispositions present from birth) and Matured Virtue (virtue in the highest sense), the latter requiring the intellectual element provided by Practical Wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children and brutes may have natural dispositions (e.g., courage impulses) but without intellectual element these can be harmful; matured virtue combines the natural state with practical wisdom, yielding true moral excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue implies possession of Right Reason (practical wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: In defining Virtue people add 'state which is accordant with Right Reason'; 'right' here means in accordance with Practical Wisdom, so Virtue implies the possession of Right Reason (practical wisdom) rather than being mere reasoning processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates was partly right (virtues are not independent of Practical Wisdom) but wrong to identify them purely with intellectual reasoning; virtue implies possession of right practical deliberative capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for demonstrative knowledge (Posterior Analytics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge produced by demonstrative reasoning (demonstration) must be drawn from premises that are true, first, and incapable of syllogistic proof, and that are better known, prior in order of time, and causes of the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A syllogism without such premisses is not demonstration and will not produce knowledge. The 'first' premises are indemonstrable principles (axioms) and must be known to exist and to be prior in causal order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief-firmness and indemonstrability of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of demonstration must be indemonstrable (cannot themselves be shown by syllogism) and causes of the conclusion; the person who has demonstrative Knowledge must believe their principles more firmly than their conclusions and must not believe more firmly the contradictories of those principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To know by demonstration one must have the principles better known (either by nature or relatively) and hold them infallibly compared to the conclusion; otherwise the reasoning fails to produce true Knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of moral defects/qualities: Vice, Imperfect Self-Control, Brutishness
rubrics_metrics.description: That which is to be avoided in moral character comes in three forms: Vice, Imperfect Self-Control (akrasia), and Brutishness. Their contraries are Virtue, Self-Control, and Superhuman (heroic/godlike) Virtue respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brutishness is rare and often found among barbarians or caused by disease/maiming; superhuman virtue (heroic) is also rare. The text will later discuss specifics of Imperfect Self-Control and its relation to other states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common statements about Self-Control and Imperfect Self-Control
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of commonly held theses about self-control: I) Self-Control and Endurance are praiseworthy; Imperfect Self-Control and Softness are blameworthy. II) Self-Control equals abiding by resolution. III) The imperfectly self-controlled act at instigation of passions despite knowing wrong. IV) Perfect Self-Mastery unites Self-Control and Endurance. V) Some confuse no self-control with imperfect self-control. VI) Debate whether the practically-wise can be imperfectly self-controlled. VII) Imperfect Self-Control is sometimes specified with respect to anger, honour, gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These serve as the phenomena/opinions to be examined and tested against experience and careful analysis; Aristotle will interrogate the nature of the ignorance or weakness involved in akrasia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socratic denial of akrasia and Aristotle's response
rubrics_metrics.description: Socrates contends there is no such state as Imperfect Self-Control (akrasia): no one acts contrary to what is best while knowing it is best; apparent akratic action is due to ignorance. Aristotle objects that this is at variance with plain facts and invites inquiry into the specific nature of the ignorance if akrasia is explained by ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This debate functions as a criterion for analyzing moral failure: either re-describe akrasia as ignorance (Socratic line) or accept a form of weakness where one acts against one's prior judgement and investigate its cognitive structure (Aristotle's approach).
